items.q: How do elite runners use vision to stay motivated?
items.a: They **hyperfocus** on the finish line or a sub-goal ahead — almost like a **spotlight on one target** — instead of scanning peripheral competition. Recalibrate the circle of light to the next point when you hit each marker.

items.q: What did Balcetis's spotlight training do in the lab?
items.a: People trained to put a **circular spotlight** on a stop sign or goal line moved **27% faster** and reported **17% less pain** on ankle-weighted high-stepping — and the proximity/ease illusion worked across fitness levels.

items.q: Can dreaming about success reduce motivation?
items.a: Yes. Gabriele Oettingen's work shows positive future visualization can **psychologically satisfy** the goal — **systolic BP drops** as the body "chills out" — so people enjoy the feeling instead of acting.

items.q: What should you plan at goal-setting time instead?
items.a: Plan the path **and** pre-plan obstacles. Michael Phelps rehearsed a **2008 goggles leak** by swimming blind and counting strokes — like knowing where life jackets are **before** the boat sinks.

items.q: How does fatigue change what goals look like?
items.a: Tired, overweight, or chronically fatigued people see **distances as farther** and **hills as steeper** — which already puts you motivationally closer to "impossible."

items.q: What did the sugar Kool-Aid study show?
items.a: Extra available energy (glucose) made the finish line **look closer** — a **visual proximity illusion** that links body fuel to how hard the goal appears.

items.q: Why do self pep talks and sticky notes often fail?
items.a: They burn **time and effort** until people burn out. Balcetis favors **low-effort, automatable vision tactics** over constant self-nagging.

items.q: Why trust data over feelings about progress?
items.a: **Faulty memory** skews assessment. Balcetis's Reporter-app random pings showed she had **practiced far more** — and an upward emotional trajectory — than she remembered before a live drum deadline.
